title: Rama, the Dawn Is Breaking
hookLine: a sage wakes two sleeping princes by a river, and his words become a temple's dawn song for the Lord
carry: hindu worship cares for god, dawn to night
tomorrow: what happened the day the wind stopped blowing?

lines: TWO PRINCES ASLEEP BY A RIVER.
cards: Before sunrise, by a river, two young princes are asleep on the ground. The sage leading them, Vishvamitra, leans over and speaks. Paraphrased: Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the eastern dawn is breaking.
Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites are waiting. It's a small moment early in Valmiki's Ramayana, a teacher waking his students. But those words didn't stay by the river.
They became the opening of a hymn sung before dawn to wake the deity. Today, the last of the sleep days: the temple's night and morning.

teach.b: The hymn is the Venkatesa Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. Suprabhatam means a good dawn.
It opens with Vishvamitra's verse, then turns to the Lord of the hill and asks him, verse after verse, to wake. At the other end of the day, some temples have a bedtime rite.
The deity is laid to rest, the lamps are lowered, a last song is sung, and the doors are shut until morning. Here is the teaching, named plainly.
In Hindu worship the deity in the temple is treated as truly present, so the whole day is seva, loving service: woken, bathed, offered food, and laid to rest.

teach.h: CARE, NOT A CLAIM OF TIREDNESS
teach.b: Tradition speaks of these rites as care, not as a claim that God gets tired: the way a beloved member of the household is served. Two more things to see. The waking is spoken.
Vishvamitra doesn't shake the princes. He tells them the dawn is here and the day has work in it.

teach.h: THE TWO ENDS FRAME THE DAY
teach.b: And the two ends of the day frame everything between. Look back over the sleep days. Kumbhakarna slept his strength away, and the Gita asked for measure.
Uddalaka's bird settled at its tether. Yajnavalkya's dreamer was self-lit; his falcon folded its wings, and every daytime name was set down. Indra nearly quit over deep sleep, and found the witness.
Kumbhakarna woke and knew the right. And here, the night and the dawn held as worship. Tomorrow, the breath, and the day the wind god stood still.

how: The Venkatesa Suprabhatam is sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in homes in the morning, and some temples close the day with a rite that lays the deity to rest.

o: a rest held as care, from a gentle night to a spoken dawn
a rite kept only by priests, closed to the household
a weakness of the gods, who must be woken each morning

games.q: the night and the dawn — tap the pairs.
p: the deity laid to rest, doors shut

s: the Venkatesa Suprabhatam opens with a verse from Valmiki's Ramayana
Vishvamitra's words to the sleeping Rama: the eastern dawn is breaking, rise.
the bedtime rite means God gets tired
tradition speaks of it as care, the way a beloved member of the household is served.
Vishvamitra wakes the princes by shaking them
he speaks: the dawn is breaking, rise, the day's rites are waiting.

games.q: you're Vishvamitra. the dawn is coming and the two princes are asleep by the river. how do you wake them?
o: speak: the dawn is breaking, rise, the day has work in it.
let them sleep through the morning.
games.why: he speaks to Rama by name, tells him the dawn is breaking, and names the work of the day. those words now open a temple's waking hymn.

practice: Picture the last moment before sleep tonight, gently, a lamp lowered, a door shut, and then the first moment of tomorrow: not shaken awake, but spoken to, with one kind sentence. Rest between the two, breathing.
If you pray, offer the night and the morning both.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. A measure, a homecoming, a self-lit dream, a falcon's nest, a witness, a giant's waking, and a temple's night and dawn. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit suprabhatam: a good dawn, the name for hymns sung to wake the deity.

carryVoice: Your line: hindu worship cares for god, dawn to night. A gentle night, and a dawn that's spoken to. Rest well, and see you at dawn.
